questions.question: Consider the array [8, 3, 5, 4, 7, 6, 1, 2]. If we use the first element (8) as pivot in QuickSort, how many elements will be in the left partition after the first partitioning step?

explanations.a: Count again. Elements less than 8 are: 3, 5, 4, 7, 6, 1, 2.
explanations.b: Close, but 7 is less than 8, so it should be included.
explanations.c: Correct! All elements except the pivot (8) are smaller: 3, 5, 4, 7, 6, 1, 2.
explanations.d: This is incorrect. Count all elements smaller than the pivot 8.

questions.question: What happens when QuickSort is applied to an already sorted array using the first element as pivot?

answers.a: It runs in O(n log n) time
answers.b: It runs in O(n²) time with maximum recursion depth
answers.d: It fails to sort the array

explanations.a: This would be ideal, but using first element as pivot on sorted array creates worst-case scenario.
explanations.b: Correct! Each partition creates one empty subarray and one subarray with (n-1) elements, leading to O(n²) time and O(n) recursion depth.
explanations.c: O(n) time is not possible for a comparison-based sorting algorithm sorting n elements.
explanations.d: QuickSort will still sort correctly, but inefficiently.

questions.question: In the Lomuto partition scheme, if we have array [4, 1, 3, 9, 7] with pivot = 4, what will be the final position of the pivot after partitioning?

explanations.a: The pivot needs to move to allow smaller elements to come before it.
explanations.b: Think about how many elements are smaller than 4 in this array.
explanations.c: Correct! Elements 1 and 3 are smaller than 4, so pivot 4 will be at index 2 after partitioning: [1, 3, 4, 9, 7].
explanations.d: This would place too many elements before the pivot.

questions.question: Which pivot selection strategy provides the best guaranteed performance for QuickSort?

explanations.a: Random pivot provides good expected performance but no guarantees.
explanations.b: Median-of-three improves average case but doesn't guarantee best performance.
explanations.c: Correct! True median selection guarantees O(n log n) time complexity as it ensures balanced partitions, though it's expensive to compute.
explanations.d: First element can lead to worst-case O(n²) performance.

questions.question: In 3-way QuickSort, how are elements partitioned relative to the pivot?

answers.a: Less than pivot, greater than pivot
answers.b: Less than pivot, equal to pivot, greater than pivot

explanations.b: Correct! 3-way partitioning creates three groups: elements less than pivot, equal to pivot, and greater than pivot. This is efficient for arrays with many duplicates.
explanations.c: 3-way QuickSort doesn't partition based on even/odd properties.
explanations.d: This is not how 3-way partitioning works.

questions.question: What is the key advantage of QuickSort over MergeSort?

answers.c: QuickSort is in-place with O(log n) space complexity

explanations.a: QuickSort is not always faster; it depends on the input and implementation.
explanations.b: QuickSort is not stable (doesn't preserve relative order of equal elements).
explanations.c: Correct! QuickSort's main advantage is that it sorts in-place with only O(log n) additional space for recursion, while MergeSort requires O(n) extra space.
explanations.d: Standard QuickSort doesn't handle duplicates better than MergeSort (though 3-way QuickSort does).

questions.question: In a hybrid QuickSort implementation, why might it switch to Insertion Sort for small subarrays?

answers.b: To reduce the recursion overhead and improve performance on small arrays

explanations.a: Both algorithms are equally accurate for sorting.
explanations.b: Correct! For small arrays (typically n < 10-20), Insertion Sort's O(n²) time is often faster in practice due to lower overhead, and it reduces recursion depth.
explanations.c: While Insertion Sort uses O(1) space, the main reason for switching is performance, not memory.
explanations.d: Switching to Insertion Sort doesn't make the overall algorithm stable.
